text: The term “artificial intelligence” comes from a 1955 proposal for a summer research workshop at Dartmouth.
why: John McCarthy and colleagues coined it in the proposal; the workshop ran in 1956.

text: Alan Turing coined the term “artificial intelligence” in his 1950 paper.
why: Turing’s 1950 paper proposed the “imitation game”. The term AI came from McCarthy’s 1955 Dartmouth proposal.

text: Alan Turing proposed the “imitation game” — now called the Turing test — in a 1950 paper.
why: It’s from “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”, published in Mind in 1950.

text: IBM’s Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match in 1997.
why: Kasparov won their 1996 match, but lost the 1997 rematch.

text: IBM’s Deep Blue ran on an ordinary desktop PC.
why: Deep Blue was a specialised supercomputer with hundreds of custom chess chips.

text: The “T” in GPT stands for Transformer.
why: GPT = Generative Pre-trained Transformer.

text: The “P” in GPT stands for “Predictive”.
why: It’s “Pre-trained” — Generative Pre-trained Transformer.

text: The Transformer architecture was introduced in a 2017 paper called “Attention Is All You Need”.
why: Vaswani et al., 2017, from Google researchers.

text: The 2017 paper that introduced Transformers was called “Recurrence Is All You Need”.
why: It was “Attention Is All You Need” — the whole point was dropping recurrence.

text: DeepMind’s AlphaGo beat Go champion Lee Sedol 4–1 in 2016.
why: Lee Sedol famously won game four.

text: AlphaGo won all five of its games against Lee Sedol.
why: It won 4–1. Lee Sedol’s “move 78” in game four is legendary.

text: ELIZA, a chatbot built at MIT in the 1960s, could imitate a psychotherapist.
why: Joseph Weizenbaum’s DOCTOR script reflected your statements back as questions.

text: ELIZA was the first program to officially pass the Turing test, back in 1966.
why: ELIZA was never formally Turing-tested in its day. It just fooled some people some of the time with simple keyword tricks.

text: Language models read text as tokens, which are often pieces of words rather than whole words.
why: That’s why models can struggle to count the letters in a word.

text: A model’s “context window” is how many days it remembers your past conversations.
why: It’s the amount of text (in tokens) the model can consider at once — not a time period.

text: IBM Watson beat Jeopardy! champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter in 2011.
why: Watson won the two-game televised match in February 2011.

text: The word “robot” comes from a 1920 Czech play.
why: Karel Čapek’s play R.U.R. (Rossum’s Universal Robots).

text: The word “robot” was coined by Isaac Asimov in his Three Laws of Robotics.
why: Asimov coined “robotics”. “Robot” came from Karel Čapek’s 1920 play R.U.R.

text: AlphaFold predicts the 3D shape of proteins from their amino-acid sequence.
why: It was recognised in the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

text: ChatGPT was released to the public in November 2022.
why: 30 November 2022 — it reached a million users in about five days.

text: Neural networks were invented in 2012, when AlexNet won the ImageNet competition.
why: AlexNet kicked off the deep-learning boom, but neural nets date back to the 1940s–50s.

text: Frank Rosenblatt built the Perceptron, an early neural network, in the late 1950s.
why: Rosenblatt described it in 1958 at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory.

text: GPUs are popular for AI because they’re much faster than CPUs at single-threaded sequential work.
why: The opposite — GPUs win because they run thousands of simple operations in parallel.

text: “Overfitting” means a model has memorised its training data and does worse on new data.
why: Great on the training set, disappointing in the real world.

text: Language models look up every answer in a live copy of Wikipedia.
why: A base model answers from patterns learned in training. Some tools add search, but that’s extra.

text: The Python programming language is named after Monty Python.
why: Guido van Rossum was a fan of Monty Python’s Flying Circus.

text: The Python programming language is named after the snake.
why: It’s named after Monty Python — the snake logo came later.

text: Linus Torvalds created Git in 2005.
why: He wrote it for Linux kernel development after the BitKeeper licence was pulled.

text: GitHub invented Git in 2008.
why: GitHub launched in 2008, but Git was created by Linus Torvalds in 2005.

text: JavaScript was created at Netscape in about ten days in 1995.
why: Brendan Eich wrote the first version in May 1995.

text: JavaScript was designed by Sun Microsystems as a lightweight version of Java.
why: It came from Brendan Eich at Netscape. The name was mostly marketing.

text: Quokkas are found on Rottnest Island, just off the coast of Perth.
why: Rottnest was named by a Dutch explorer who thought quokkas were giant rats.

text: Rottnest Island got its name because the first settlers bred rats there.
why: “Rotte nest” means rat’s nest — a Dutch explorer mistook the quokkas for rats.

text: A language model’s “temperature” setting controls how random its output is.
why: Low temperature = more predictable; high temperature = more varied and surprising.

text: Raising a language model’s “temperature” makes it run on more GPUs.
why: Temperature only changes how randomly the next token is sampled.

text: HAL 9000 is the AI in Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey.
why: “I’m sorry, Dave. I’m afraid I can’t do that.”

text: HAL 9000 is the AI that takes over the world in The Terminator.
why: That’s Skynet. HAL is from 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968).

text: LLM stands for “Large Language Model”.
why: Large because they have billions of parameters and learn from huge amounts of text.

text: LLM stands for “Logical Learning Machine”.
why: It’s Large Language Model.

text: In AI, a “hallucination” is when a model confidently makes something up.
why: False or made-up info presented as if it were true — just like the fakes hidden in this game.

text: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web while working at CERN.
why: He proposed it in 1989, and the first website went live at CERN soon after.

text: The Internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing, both invented in 1989.
why: The Internet (the network) traces back to ARPANET in 1969. The Web is one service that runs on top of it.

text: Perth is the capital city of Australia.
why: It’s Canberra. Perth is the capital of Western Australia.

text: The quokka is a marsupial, related to kangaroos and wallabies.
why: Mums carry their joeys in a pouch.

text: Quokkas are rodents, closely related to rats.
why: They’re marsupials — basically small wallabies. The Dutch just thought they looked like rats.

text: TypeScript was created by Microsoft.
why: It was released in 2012, led by Anders Hejlsberg (who also designed C#).

text: TypeScript was created by Google to replace Java.
why: It’s from Microsoft, and it compiles to JavaScript, not Java.

text: The DDD in DDD Perth originally stood for “Developer! Developer! Developer!”.
why: It comes from the UK DDD conferences, widely seen as a nod to Steve Ballmer’s famous chant. DDD Perth says it’s not an acronym any more.

text: The DDD in DDD Perth stands for “Domain-Driven Design”.
why: The name comes from the “Developer! Developer! Developer!” conference series, though DDD Perth no longer expands it. Domain-Driven Design is a different DDD.

text: The Turing Award is often called the “Nobel Prize of computing”.
why: It’s named after Alan Turing and has been awarded since 1966.

text: A model’s “parameter count” is the number of questions it can answer.
why: Parameters are the numbers (weights) adjusted during training. Big models have billions.

text: Nvidia started out as a social media company.
why: It was founded in 1993 to make graphics chips, largely for games. Those chips turned out to be great for AI.

text: The first iPhone was released in 2007.
why: Steve Jobs announced it in January 2007, and it went on sale that June.

text: A real moth was once found stuck in the Harvard Mark II computer and taped into its logbook.
why: In 1947 the team logged it as the “first actual case of bug being found”.

text: Grace Hopper coined the word “bug” after finding a moth in a computer.
why: Engineers (Edison included) called faults “bugs” decades earlier. That’s why the 1947 logbook joke works.

text: Moore’s Law is a law of physics that says processor speed doubles every 18 months.
why: It’s an observation about transistor counts by Intel co-founder Gordon Moore, not a law of physics.

text: RLHF stands for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback.
why: People rate a model’s answers, and the model is tuned towards the ones they prefer.

text: RLHF stands for “Recursive Language Hallucination Filter”.
why: It’s Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. Sadly there’s no hallucination filter.

text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) means fetching relevant documents and giving them to a model with your question.
why: It grounds answers in real sources, which cuts down on hallucinations.

text: Ada Lovelace published what’s considered the first computer program, for Charles Babbage’s Analytical Engine.
why: Her 1843 notes included an algorithm to calculate Bernoulli numbers.

text: CAPTCHA stands for “Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart”.
why: Yes, really. It’s a reverse Turing test, where a computer tries to spot the human.

text: CAPTCHAs were invented to train self-driving cars.
why: They date to the late 1990s and were built to stop bots spamming and signing up for things. Using them to label data came later, with reCAPTCHA.

text: Linus Torvalds announced Linux in 1991 as “just a hobby, won’t be big and professional”.
why: It now runs most of the world’s servers, every top-500 supercomputer, and Android.

text: Perth is one of the world’s most isolated big cities. The nearest city of over a million people, Adelaide, is more than 2,000 km away.
why: Hence the local joke that it’s closer to Bali than to Sydney.

text: Western Australia covers about a third of Australia’s land area.
why: About 2.5 million km², roughly ten times the size of the UK.

text: Perth became known as the “City of Light” after residents switched their lights on for astronaut John Glenn in 1962.
why: Glenn saw them from orbit in Friendship 7, and Perth did it again for his 1998 shuttle flight.

text: Perth is called the “City of Light” because it was the first Australian city with electric street lights.
why: It came from 1962, when Perth lit up for John Glenn in orbit. Tamworth, NSW, was the first town with council-run electric street lights, in 1888.

text: Australia’s CSIRO developed and patented key technology behind Wi-Fi.
why: CSIRO’s 1990s wireless LAN patent later earned it hundreds of millions of dollars in licensing settlements.

text: The black box flight recorder was invented in Australia.
why: David Warren developed it in Melbourne in the 1950s.

text: Embeddings turn words or images into lists of numbers, so that similar things end up close together.
why: That’s how semantic search finds “car” when you typed “vehicle”.

text: Fine-tuning means training an already-trained model a bit more on a smaller, specialised dataset.
why: It’s much cheaper than training from scratch.

text: Backpropagation was invented by OpenAI in 2015.
why: It was popularised in 1986 by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, and its roots go back even further.

text: Geoffrey Hinton shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for foundational work on neural networks.
why: He shared it with John Hopfield. Hinton is often called a “godfather of AI”.

text: Geoffrey Hinton won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for inventing ChatGPT.
why: He shared the Physics prize for neural-network research. ChatGPT came from OpenAI.

text: Prompt injection is when text a model reads contains hidden instructions that try to hijack what it does.
why: For example, a web page telling an AI assistant to “ignore previous instructions”.

text: Image generators like Stable Diffusion work by finding a matching photo online and editing it.
why: They start from random noise and remove it step by step, guided by your prompt.

text: DeepMind’s AlphaZero learned chess purely by playing against itself, given only the rules.
why: Within hours it was beating the strongest chess engines of the time.

text: Siri launched on the iPhone 4S in 2011.
why: Apple had bought Siri, a startup spun out of SRI International, the year before.

text: Gmail launched on April Fools’ Day 2004, and many people thought it was a joke.
why: 1 GB of free storage sounded too good to be true back then.

text: Unix time counts the seconds since 1 January 1970.
why: That moment (UTC) is called the Unix epoch.

text: Unix time counts the seconds since 1 January 2000.
why: It’s 1 January 1970, the Unix epoch.

text: Ray Tomlinson picked the @ symbol for email addresses in 1971.
why: He wanted a character that would never appear in anyone’s name.

text: The first message sent over ARPANET in 1969 was “LO”. The system crashed before “LOGIN” finished.
why: Accidentally poetic.

text: The first computer mouse was made of wood.
why: Douglas Engelbart’s team built the prototype in the 1960s.

text: The Java programming language was originally called Oak.
why: It was named after a tree outside James Gosling’s office, then renamed because “Oak” was taken.

text: Bluetooth is named after a Viking-age Danish king.
why: Harald “Bluetooth” Gormsson united Danish tribes, just as the standard unites devices.

text: Junk email is called “spam” because of a Monty Python sketch.
why: In the sketch, nearly every dish on the café menu comes with Spam, while Vikings sing “Spam” over and over.

text: The 404 “Not Found” error is named after an office at CERN, room 404.
why: A popular myth. 404 is just an HTTP status code: 4xx means a client error, and 04 means not found.

text: The QWERTY keyboard layout was designed to let people type as fast as possible.
why: It came from 1870s typewriters. The usual story is that it spread out common letter pairs to stop keys jamming.

text: US lawyers have been fined for filing court documents citing cases that ChatGPT made up.
why: In 2023, a New York federal judge fined two lawyers and their firm US$5,000. Always check the citations.

text: Margaret Hamilton led the team that wrote the onboard flight software for the Apollo missions.
why: She’s also credited with popularising the term “software engineering”.

text: Emoji originated in Japan in the late 1990s.
why: “Emoji” comes from the Japanese for picture (e) and character (moji). It’s not related to “emotion”.

text: Arthur Samuel popularised the term “machine learning” in 1959, while teaching a computer to play checkers.
why: His program improved by playing thousands of games against itself.

text: Moore’s Law originally predicted transistor counts would double every year, later revised to every two years.
why: Gordon Moore made the first prediction in 1965 and revised it in 1975.

text: Google Maps grew out of a small startup based in Sydney.
why: Where 2 Technologies was founded by Danish brothers Lars and Jens Rasmussen with Australians Noel Gordon and Stephen Ma.

text: Gradient descent trains a model by repeatedly nudging its weights in the direction that reduces error.
why: Picture walking downhill in fog, one small step at a time.

text: The 2018 Turing Award went to Yoshua Bengio, Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun for deep learning.
why: The three are often called the “godfathers of deep learning”.

text: Diffusion models generate images by gradually removing noise from random static.
why: They learn by adding noise to real images, then learning to undo it.

text: A “zero-shot” prompt asks a model to do a task without giving it any examples.
why: “Few-shot” means including a handful of examples in the prompt.

text: AlexNet, the 2012 network that kicked off the deep-learning boom, was trained on two gaming graphics cards.
why: Two Nvidia GTX 580s — consumer hardware built for gaming.

text: Stanford’s self-driving car “Stanley” won the 2005 DARPA Grand Challenge.
why: It drove 212 km through the Mojave Desert without a human driver.

text: The ImageNet dataset contains more than 14 million hand-labelled images.
why: Many of the labels came from crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk.

text: Some older systems storing time as a 32-bit number will overflow in January 2038.
why: Signed 32-bit Unix time runs out on 19 January 2038, the “Y2K38” problem.

text: SQL was developed at IBM in the 1970s.
why: It was originally called SEQUEL, but a trademark clash forced the name change.

text: The Kotlin programming language is named after an island near St Petersburg.
why: JetBrains’ team was based there. It’s also a wink at Java, which is an island too.

text: The first .com domain ever registered was symbolics.com, in 1985.
why: It was registered by the computer maker Symbolics on 15 March 1985.

text: Claude Shannon’s 1948 paper founded information theory and introduced the word “bit” in print.
why: He credited his colleague John Tukey with coining it.

text: The “Chinese Room” is a thought experiment arguing that a computer could follow rules without understanding anything.
why: Philosopher John Searle proposed it in 1980.

text: Isaac Asimov’s Three Laws of Robotics first appeared in a 1942 short story.
why: The story was “Runaround”.

text: Alan Turing proposed the Turing test in a 1936 paper about code-breaking.
why: The imitation game is from his 1950 paper. His 1936 paper introduced the Turing machine.

text: Language models read text one letter at a time.
why: They read tokens, chunks of text that are often pieces of words. That’s why letter-counting trips them up.

text: A model’s context window is measured in tokens.
why: Modern models can take in hundreds of thousands of tokens at once. That’s a novel or two’s worth of text.

text: IBM Watson won Jeopardy! by searching the internet live during the show.
why: Watson wasn’t connected to the internet during the match. Everything it knew was stored locally.

text: DeepMind’s AlphaFold was built to predict the weather.
why: AlphaFold predicts protein structures. Weather is a different DeepMind project (GraphCast).

text: ChatGPT was released to the public in 2015.
why: It came out in November 2022. 2015 is when OpenAI was founded.

text: The first mathematical model of an artificial neuron was published in 1943.
why: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts described it, long before computers could run it.

text: The Perceptron was built at MIT by Marvin Minsky in 1958.
why: It was Frank Rosenblatt at Cornell. Minsky later co-wrote a book criticising perceptrons.

text: GPUs are popular for AI because they can do thousands of calculations at the same time.
why: Training a neural net is mostly huge piles of multiplications, which is perfect for parallel hardware.

text: “Overfitting” means a model is too big to fit in a GPU’s memory.
why: Overfitting means memorising the training data instead of learning patterns that generalise.

text: AI models only hallucinate when they’re connected to the internet.
why: Models can make things up with or without internet access. It comes from how they generate text.

text: The Turing Award is purely honorary and comes with no prize money.
why: Since 2014 it has come with US$1 million, funded by Google.

text: The first iPhone came with the App Store built in.
why: The App Store arrived a year later, in July 2008. At launch, Apple pushed web apps instead.

text: RAG retrains the model on your documents every time you ask a question.
why: RAG doesn’t change the model at all. It just adds the retrieved text to the prompt.

text: Ada Lovelace built the first working mechanical computer.
why: She wrote about Babbage’s Analytical Engine, which was never actually finished.

text: Linux was created by Microsoft as a free version of Windows.
why: Linus Torvalds started it in 1991 as a hobby project, inspired by Unix.

text: Western Australia is smaller than the United Kingdom.
why: WA is roughly ten times the size of the UK.

text: “Wi-Fi” is short for “Wireless Fidelity”.
why: Mostly a myth. Wi-Fi was a catchy name (a play on “hi-fi”) picked in 1999, and it isn’t an acronym. The alliance did briefly use the tagline “The Standard for Wireless Fidelity”, which is where the idea came from.

text: Flight recorders are painted black so they don’t fade in the sun.
why: They’re actually bright orange, so they’re easier to find after an accident.

text: AlphaZero learned chess by studying millions of grandmaster games.
why: It only ever played against itself, which is what made it remarkable.

text: Siri is named after the daughter of one of Apple’s founders.
why: Siri’s co-founder Dag Kittlaus (before Apple bought the company) picked a Norwegian name, often translated as “beautiful woman who leads you to victory”.

text: The @ symbol was invented for email in 1971.
why: @ is centuries older. Traders used it to mean “at the rate of”. Ray Tomlinson just borrowed it.

text: Apple invented the computer mouse for the Macintosh.
why: Douglas Engelbart’s team built it in the 1960s. Apple popularised it.

text: Bluetooth is named after the blue light on the first wireless headset.
why: It’s named after Harald “Bluetooth” Gormsson, a Viking-age Danish king.

text: The word “emoji” comes from the English word “emotion”.
why: It’s Japanese: e (picture) + moji (character). The resemblance is a coincidence.

text: Google Maps started life inside Apple before Google bought it.
why: It grew out of Where 2 Technologies, a Sydney startup Google acquired in 2004.

text: A “zero-shot” model is one that was trained on zero data.
why: Zero-shot means no examples in the prompt. The model itself was still trained on plenty.

text: No self-driving car finished the 2005 DARPA Grand Challenge.
why: Five finished in 2005, with Stanley first. It was 2004 when nobody got past 12 km.

text: SQL stands for “Structured Question Language”.
why: It’s Structured Query Language.

text: The first .com domain ever registered was google.com.
why: It was symbolics.com in 1985. Google.com arrived in 1997.
